Investigations are systematically designed to determine the presence of liver disease, classify the type of injury (hepatocellular vs. cholestatic), evaluate synthetic function, and identify the specific etiology.
Markers of Hepatocellular Injury (Aminotransferases) Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT): Primarily localized to the liver cytosol; highly specific for hepatic parenchymal injury.
Aspartate Aminotransferase (AST): Present in liver (cytosol and mitochondria), cardiac muscle, skeletal muscle, kidneys, and brain.

Clinical Interpretation of Aminotransferase Elevations: Marked elevation (>1000 U/L): Suggests acute ischemic injury (shock liver), acute viral hepatitis, or toxin/ drug-induced liver injury (e.g., acetaminophen toxicity).
Mild-to-moderate elevation (<300 U/L): Common in Chronic Hepatitis B/C, Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD/MASLD), and Alcoholic Liver Disease.
AST:ALT Ratio (De Ritis Ratio): An AST:ALT ratio > 2:1 is highly suggestive of alcoholic liver disease, driven by pyridoxal-5-phosphate deficiency in alcoholics which selectively suppresses ALT.
A ratio > 1 in chronic viral hepatitis suggests progression to cirrhosis.

In clinical practice, liver diseases usually manifest as acute hepatitis, chronic liver disease/cirrhosis, cholestasis (obstructive or hepatocellular), or incidental abnormalities discovered on routine screening.

True Markers of Hepatic Synthetic Capacity Serum Albumin: Synthesized exclusively by the liver.
Because it has a long half-life (~20 days), low serum albumin is characteristic of chronic liver disease (e.g., cirrhosis) or severe protein-losing states, rather than acute liver injury.
